newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles flock to big mass on last day of Papal visit.
newsitem.headline: Poles flock to big mass on last day of Papal visit.

text.p: Pope John Paul presided at a big open-air mass before half a million people on Tuesday as he prepared to return to the Vatican at the end of a triumphant tour of his homeland.
The mass at the airport of Krosno in southeast Poland, where the Pope canonised 15th century Franciscan holy man John of Dukla, was the last major ceremony of his 11-day visit.
Jan of Dukla helped his people repel a Tartar attack on Lvov, now part of Ukraine, in 1474.
In his sermon before the crowd, spread out over many acres, the Pope praised the saint for his patriotism as well as modern church leaders who had stood up to communism in this century.
He urged Poles, particularly those in rural areas, to hold on to their 1,000-year-old Christian traditions in face of mounting secularism including that spread by the mass media.
"Do not let them be taken away from you. Some people are trying to do so. The world is full of dangers," the Pope said.
The mass attracted the second largest crowd of the trip after one which drew more than 1.5 million to Krakow on Sunday.

During his trip the Pope has repeatedly paid tribute to the faithful and the Church hierarchy for holding fast while Marxist regimes before 1989 curtailed Church freedom and denied permission to build new places of worship.

The journey has often deeply moved the 77-year-old Pontiff and challenged Poles to ponder how they should use freedoms he helped them to win through his support for the Solidarity free trade union's struggle for democracy against communism.
The Pope was flying by helicopter to Krakow on Tuesday afternoon and returning to Rome in the evening.
"He is not a sentimental man, he is too sophisticated for that," chief Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said when asked whether the Pope was sad at the thought of leaving.
"But he has a strong capacity to be moved by emotions," Navarro-Valls added.

The last leg of the trip through 12 towns and cities took the Pope to the southern highlands near his birthplace of Wadowice, and to Krakow where he rose from student to Cardinal and which he left in 1978 for his unexpected election as Pontiff.

On Monday he prayed at the grave in Krakow of his mother, father and brother whose loss before he was 21 hurt him deeply. Earlier, visiting his former university, he recalled the day wartime Nazi occupiers took its professors to a concentration camp.
The Pope has attracted crowds estimated by the Church at around six million. He repeatedly told his compatriots their freedom was meaningless if not shaped by moral values.

"When there is a void in the area of values -- when chaos and confusion reign in the moral sphere -- freedom dies, man is reduced from freedom to slavery, becoming a slave to passions and pseudo-values," he said during a mass near the start.
On June 3 in Gniezno, where the presidents of seven nations gathered to hear him, the Pope also warned of an invisible new wall of "economic and political selfishness" dividing Europe.
He said no countries should be excluded from communities now arising on the continent and stated "There will be no European unity unless it is based on unity of the spirit."
Nowhere did the Pope challenge current Polish values more strongly than over the law, introduced last year, allowing abortion in cases of a woman's financial or other hardship.
He said societies allowing abortion were barbarous and on Monday he praised doctors who refused to conduct abortions which the Catholic Church views as the killing of children.

These and other comments addressed highly political matters as campaigning gets underway for parliamentary elections due in September that will pit pro-Catholic, anti-abortion rightist opposition parties against the ruling ex-communists.

Although rightist groups gathered around Solidarity hope the impact of the Pope's visit will help bring them victory, even chiefs of the ex-communists paid tribute to the calming effects of his presence on political rows raging in Poland.
